content: This is the discussion thread for Hex, following the announcement at #Project announcements > Hex: a computational algebra library .

I'll just begin by noting that there are probably some exciting quirks in this library, as I've made extensive use of AI in implementing the specs. Nevertheless, I'm excited by how well the spec-driven development process has gone, and I'm pleased by how much has been possible with relatively limited time. In particular the proofs are not intended for human consumption! Please point out quirks, gross errors, and future improvements in a constructive fashion. :-)
There's an example in the manual demonstrating using LLL to do a Coppersmith-style attack on RSA.

To say something about the "without mathlib computations" and "with mathlib theory" split. One motivation for this design is that it makes it relatively easier for Mathlib to adopt pieces of Hex if it wants to (e.g. a factorize_poly tactic that produces a factorization, and proofs of irreducibility of the factors, is not so hard from here). We would just add the computation libraries as upstream dependencies, and then just absorb the relevant HexXMathlib libraries into Mathlib.

From the announcement

  • Lean and Isabelle implementations which call out to fplll via an FFI shim, and then fully verify the result.

Is the verification algorithm also proven correct by lean, like the native implementation?

I don't know much about computational number theory, but there are a lot of optimized C libraries like https://flintlib.org/ so it would be great to be able to use them in verified lean proofs. Do you know/expect most computational problems to go this route - ffi to optimized OSS solver and proved verifier in lean? Is that even possible that often, I assume for some algorithms verifying a solution might be as hard as finding one? Is certified lean computation (for direct computation or for verification of an proposed solution) incompatible with probablistic algorithms like Pollard's Rho?

Rado Kirov said:

Is the verification algorithm also proven correct by lean, like the native implementation?

Yes.

When reading up about decidable equality for algebraic numbers I saw that the lll algorithm was recommended. I also see isolation of roots. Do these libraries enable decidable equality for algebraic numbers?

Rado Kirov said:

Is that even possible that often, I assume for some algorithms verifying a solution might be as hard as finding one?

Yes, anything is possible here. Some problems have easy-to-check certificates (perhaps hard to compute), and some problems don't admit certificates at all. There's no particular problem with probabilistic algorithms --- you can't feed them into the decide mechanism, which really does have to decide (i.e. it has no "I'm not sure" option, although this has been discussed), but generally you can wrap such algorithms in tactics that just fail sometimes.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

Do these libraries enable decidable equality for algebraic numbers?

Not yet: we have lll implemented here in Hex, but the algebraic number part of the library isn't implemented yet. But yes, decidable equality is part of the plan. (A draft of the spec for this is already written; I need to update it a bit based on some feedback, but they're still mostly the plan.)

(I'm going to release a integer polynomial factorization library, using Berlekamp-Zassenhaus + van Hoeij lattice based reconstruction, before I get to the algebraic number stuff. BZ is working+verified, but needs tuning and some tactic layers before it's ready for release.)
